scope: Twenty-fifth expansion batch: 12 controlled possible-versus-desired extent exercises in six matched verb pairs (read, write, transport, use, send, talk). Six possible-extent answers share potential + kagiri/dake; six desired-extent answers use tai + dake. Three possible model buttons show kagiri and three show dake, not independent discrimination between the two.

sources.section: Actual heading かぎり【限り】, sense2c for the whole of a range and2d for the fullest extent/up to a limit, including chikara-no-kagiri. Sense3 separately covers continuing conditions. Not the separate giri entry or archaic funeral senses. This supports maximum-extent meaning and the distinction from an ongoing condition, not an unrestricted substitution rule with dake.

Actual heading だけ［副助］, sense1 amount/degree/limit with hashireru-dake hashitte-miyou and gloss kagiri; sense2 separately describes restriction. The dictionary's examples and gloss support possible extent rather than an assumption that dake always means a small quantity. Other proportional/conditional senses are not replaced by this batch.

Actual meaning/usage and detailed grammar sections explicitly contrast potential + dake (up to the available limit) with tai + dake (until the desired amount is satisfied). Inspected chair-arrangement, sending available inventory and using paper examples, plus the formation chart. Repeating the action verb is the pattern illustrated here, not a claim that every possible use of dake requires immediate repetition.

Actual meaning gives the utmost possible extent; formation lists verb dictionary form and noun-no. Simplified extraction omitted examples, so actual HTML was inspected: dekiru-kagiri-no-koto-wa-shita with possible failure, chikara-no-kagiri, dekiru-kagiri as an action modifier, and ikeru-kagiri-no-tokoro-made. Broad life advice and a typo in an unrelated example are not adopted. Maximum effort does not guarantee success.

sources.publisher: Tokyo University of Foreign Studies, Japanese Grammar Module
sources.section: Section1, group1 formation u to eru, with kaku to kakeru. All six supplied verbs are godan and follow this formation. Other verb groups and the later ra-drop discussion are not made new targets.
Actual About: tai attaches to the masu stem and expresses a wanted action. Only this attachment is used; blanket person restrictions and claims about ga always intensifying desire are not adopted.
Exact 限り/kagiri, extent/scope and as-much-as/to-the-limits senses; not the separate kiri reading or only-once suffix use.
Exact particle 丈/dake, sense2 as much as/to the extent of, usually written in kana. Not the mountain noun or suffix dake. Recognized spelling is accepted without a frequency claim.
Exact 読む/yomu, godan-mu read sense. The 訓む note belongs to the separate native-reading sense and is not imported into story-reading answers.
Exact 書く/kaku, godan-ku write/compose sense, not drawing.
Exact 運ぶ/hakobu, godan-bu transitive carry/transport sense, not intransitive progress or honorific coming.

Exact 使う/遣う, tsukau, godan-u use/consume senses without spelling restriction. Accept the corresponding potential/tai spellings while retaining ordinary 使う in models; dictionary recognition is not proof of equal frequency.
Exact 送る/okuru, godan-ru send/transmit sense, not escorting or spending one's life.

Exact 話す/咄す, hanasu, godan-su talk/tell senses without spelling restriction. Corresponding potential/tai forms are accepted; models use ordinary 話す, and acceptance of 咄す is not a usage-frequency recommendation.

authoringNotes: All scenarios are original and need independent linguistic review. Dictionaries and teaching patterns support the meanings and recognized forms, not automatic idiomaticity of every invented clause. Review every accepted completion in its full context.

The question-side task names nonpast potential + kagiri or dake versus tai + dake of the supplied verb, with kana/kanji permitted. Only the first phrase is missing; the repeated main verb is printed. Include all fitting verb/particle spelling combinations; do not put a fitting kagiri/dake equivalent on a wrong button.

Six possible-extent items share one target; three model labels use kagiri and three use dake. They are not independently tested word choices. Six reciprocal desired-extent items retain the same verbs and contrasting model options.

The actual scenarios separate desire and possibility: in every possible-extent item, the desired amount exceeds what is available; in every desired-extent item, the person stops below what remains available. The reading pair even reaches the same three-story outcome for different reasons. Do not generalize from these constructed contrasts that the two bounds can never coincide.

Possibility is relative to today's access, field space, vehicle/trip capacity, usable supply, daily service quota or allotted speaking time. It is not restricted to physical skill, and 'as much as possible' does not demand unsafe exertion, impossible speaking speed or exploration of every alternative service. No named real service's quota is asserted.

Kagiri here describes the fullest available extent in a bounded episode, not merely the ongoing condition 'as long as the ability exists'. Dake is not equated with a small amount. The earlier article's conditional/evidential kagiri and desired/correlated dake examples remain intact.

Noun-based chikara-no-kagiri and generic dekiru-dake/kagiri are explained as related patterns, not counted as independently tested exercises. Kurai degree/minimum and broader mixed selection remain separate follow-ups. The category distinction is preserved: kagiri's noun-based use versus particle dake, not a claim that similar meanings imply identical parts of speech.

Fuller paraphrases with dekiru, hitsuyou-na, suki-na or other verbs, past-potential and other tense forms, and added particles lie outside this explicitly named basic-form task, not outside grammatical Japanese. A desired amount need not always be smaller than capacity, and maximum available effort need not achieve a larger intended goal.

Retrieval pitfalls: an initially guessed Kotobank numeric URL resolved to 掻き捨て, not 限り. The actual kagiri page above was found by its verified citation and heading. Search summaries supplied mismatched URLs and unsupported book/publisher claims, which were not used. Bunpro's dake extraction returned a forum post rather than the main lesson. Japanistry's inspected page illustrates the same repetition pattern but its universal immediate-repetition rule and complete-interchangeability claim for narubeku/dekiru-dake are not adopted.

All317 previous exercise records and IDs are preserved. The article gains one scoped subsection and one reference bullet, with matching README/contract coverage and focused regressions. No Android, counter, schema, grading or SRS changes; one identity covers each exercise's spelling and presentation alternatives.
